sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The domain of active strike-slip deformation in NW and W Slovenia is positioned between the S vergent thrust domain in the Friuli area of NE Italy and SW verging thrusting domain of the Dinarides. Earthquake and geology data in NE Italy indicate that the prevailing mechanism of deformation is thrusting on E-W oriented planes whereas dextral-reverse and purely dextral strike-slip displacements on NNW-SSE oriented planes occur further E and SE. The prevailing fault orientation in the Dinarides is in the orogen-parallel NW-SE direction. Earthquakes and geologic data along these faults exhibit thrust focal mechanisms in the southern and central parts of the Dinarides, and dextral-reverse mechanisms in the northern Dinarides. The first stage of mountain building connected to the South Alpine orogeny is Eocene thrusting and reverse fault movements along the NE Adriatic margin. During the Eocene to Lower Miocene, NE-SW directed shortening led to thrusting and uplift along SW vergent NW-SE oriented faults in the Central and External Dinarides (e.g. Tari and Pamic, 1998; Pamic et al., 2002), Julian and Friuli Alps, and E Dolomites (Doglioni, 1987). The Eocene Dinaric faults were strongly dismembered by younger, mostly late Oligocene and Miocene, south-vergent South-Alpine thrusts and steep reverse faults, which resulted in overthrusting and refolding of Dinaric structures both in the Friuli region (Doglioni, 1987; Nussbaum, 2000) and in the Julian Alps (Placer and Car, 1998). During Late Oligocene-Miocene South Alpine shortening resulted in formation of E-W oriented thrust and reverse faults. During the Miocene?Pliocene transition, the Alpine region was subjected to a change in regional style of deformation probably due to termination of subduction and slab pull along the eastern edge of the Carpathians (Horvath and Cloetingh, 1996). This change in the regional stress field coupled with the continuous northward motion of Adria resulted in inversion and reactivation of previous favourably oriented structures. The NW-SE steep-dipping fault planes exhibiting dextral strike-slip kinematics show reactivation of older NE-SE oriented thrust/reverse faults (Kastelic et al., 2008). The majority of regional seismicity is concentrated on N and E margins of the Adria and the region of W Julian Alps together with Friuli-Venezia Giulia, represents seismically most active area in the entire Alpine region. The Idrija Fault is responsible for the strongest event recorded in the region that occured on March 26th 1511, as well as an M 5.8 event of January 1st 1926. The Ravne Fault, that lies just 8 km to the north and exhibits same geometrical and mechanical characteristics as the Idtija Fault has hosted moderate sized earthquakes in 1998 and 2004 with magnitude values of 5.7 and 5.2 respectivately. Approximately 30 km to the E lies the source of the 1976 Gemona earthquake that occurred on an E-W oriented thrust plane. Such source lies on the NW-SE trending, dextral strike-slip Idrija Fault that in its NW part runs through the eastern part of the Southern Alps, while at its SE end extends to the unit of Dinarides. This source runs along the strike of the Idrija fault system, that exhibits right-stepping segmentation along its trace. The northwestern boundary of the source is in the area of interaction between the E-W trending Gemona-Kobarid thrust with the NW-SE oriented strand of the Idrija Fault System. The activity of the south-eastern part of the source is testified by moderate historical and instrumental seismicity. The Mw 5.8 1926 Cerknica earthquake is located in the area of a segment stepover zone.
This Source represents a reactivated thrust fault of Cretaceous limestones on Eocen flysch rocks. The seismogenically, present day, active fault runs in the fault zone of the old thrust fault zone, but exhibits steeper dips and strike-slip sense of fault displacement.
We inferred the depth interval of this Source from geological and seismological data. We heve obtained the average strike and dip of the source on the basis of published geologic maps (Buser, 1964; Placer, 2008; Placer et al., 2010), while average rake of the source was infered from seismological and geological data. Values of minimum and maximum slip rates were inferred from geodynamic data (Kastelic and Carafa, 2012) and geological considerations for the regional data. Maximum magnitude of the source was assigned considering the fault geometry and regional geodynamic conditions.

pictures.t: Long-term fault slip rates for the External Dinarides
pictures.c: Average long-term fault slip rates for the External Dinarides (Kastelic and Carafa, 2012). The width of each colored band is proportional to long-term slip rate. The blue and green bands represent thrust and dextral strike-slip faulting, respectively. The numerical values plotted above the fault traces are the average slip rates for each fault element. Each active fault is coded with its corresponding alphanumeric value.
